bibliographic.title: Online Health Information–Seeking in the Era of Large Language Models: Cross-Sectional Web-Based Survey Study
bibliographic.citation_apa: Yun, H. S., & Bickmore, T. (2025). Online health information–seeking in the era of large language models: Cross-sectional web-based survey study. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 27, e68560. https://doi.org/10.2196/68560

methodology.study_design: cross-sectional web-based survey of crowd workers via Prolific
methodology.sample_description: Crowd workers recruited through Prolific; questionnaire covered sociodemographic information, trust in health care providers, eHealth literacy, AI attitudes, chronic health condition status, and online health information source use, perceptions, and actions
methodology.technology_context: LLM-based chatbots such as ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot used for online health information seeking

eligibility.decision_rationale: The study is an empirical survey of user patterns, perceptions, and actions when seeking health information from LLM-based chatbots in a regulated health context. It provides supporting evidence on safety risks, trust, cross-checking, and cautious adherence, but the provided text does not examine conversational governance mechanisms such as guardrails, observability, audit, compliance controls, institutional oversight, or operational governance of LLM conversational systems.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only front matter and partial methods are available; full-text review is needed to confirm whether the article discusses governance, oversight, or compliance mechanisms beyond end-user verification behavior.

appraisal.notes: Clear cross-sectional survey design with named instruments (eHEALS, T-HCT, AIAS-4) and quantified results. Sampling relies on Prolific crowd workers, limiting generalizability. Ethics and study limitations are not visible in the provided excerpts.

cerqual.explanation: Findings are internally coherent and adequately reported for a behavioral survey, but methodological limitations include a convenience sample of crowd workers. Relevance to conversational governance is partial because the study focuses on consumer information-seeking behavior rather than governance architecture, compliance, or system-level oversight.

coding.theme: Consumer use and cautious uptake of LLM-based health information
coding.subtheme: Verification, trust, and adherence differences across information sources

synthesis.main_claim: LLM-based chatbots are an emerging but minority source for online health information; users show more cautious cross-checking and lower adherence to chatbot advice than to search engines or health websites, while younger age and more positive AI attitudes correlate with greater chatbot use.
synthesis.contribution: Provides empirical survey evidence on how users perceive, validate, and act on health information from LLM-based chatbots compared with traditional online sources in a healthcare context.
synthesis.limitations: Based on a Prolific crowd-worker sample; only abstract and partial methods are available in the supplied text; does not assess institutional or technical governance mechanisms for conversational AI.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as supporting evidence on end-user verification behavior, trust, safety risk awareness, and cautious adherence in regulated health contexts involving LLM chatbots; not central evidence for conversational governance frameworks or operational controls.

evidence.claim: Study focuses on LLM-based chatbots for online health information seeking
evidence.excerpt: As large language model (LLM)–based chatbots such as ChatGPT (OpenAI) grow in popularity, it is essential to understand their role in delivering online health information

evidence.claim: Regulated health context with safety risk concern
evidence.excerpt: These chatbots often generate inaccurate content, posing potential safety risks.

evidence.claim: Empirical cross-sectional web survey design with defined sample size
evidence.excerpt: Methods: A web-based survey of crowd workers was conducted via Prolific.

evidence.claim: Human verification behavior is measured via cross-checking
evidence.excerpt: For information obtained from LLM-based chatbots, 19.4% (12/63) of participants cross-checked the information

evidence.claim: Users are more cautious with chatbot advice than other online sources
evidence.excerpt: the adherence to health information from LLM-based chatbots seemed more cautious compared to search engines or health-related websites.

evidence.claim: Transparency is framed as important for risk mitigation
evidence.excerpt: enhancing their accuracy and transparency will be essential in mitigating any potential risks by supporting responsible information-seeking

evidence.claim: Questionnaire includes validated trust and AI attitude scales
evidence.excerpt: the full eHealth Literacy Scale (eHEALS) [25], Trust in the Health Care Team (T-HCT) Scale [26], the 4-item Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale (AIAS-4) [27]

evidence.claim: Professional consultation is preferred validation source over AI tools
evidence.excerpt: The preferred source for validating information from the internet was consulting health care professionals (40/132, 30.3%), while only a very small percentage of participants (5/214, 2.3%) consulted AI tools to cross-check information
